Some Christians understand the first light as a distinct, temporary light; others read the sequence as a theological or literary ordering rather than a scientific timeline. Either way, Genesis directs us to the Creator as the source of life and order.

Jesus has explained that people need new life from the Spirit, and that the Son of Man must be “lifted up” so that those who believe may have eternal life (John 3:3–15). “The world” points to the reach of God’s love—not just one nation or group. “Believe in him” means more than knowing facts about Jesus; it is entrusting yourself to him. Eternal life is life with God, beginning now and lasting beyond death.

The verse does not say that God loves people because they have earned it. It presents his gift as the expression of his love. That can be a deep encouragement: you are invited to receive life through Jesus, not to prove yourself worthy of God’s care.

text:
Micah 6:8 turns faith into three everyday practices: **act justly, love mercy, and walk humbly with God**. This week, try making each one concrete:

- **Act justly:** Notice one situation where someone is being overlooked or treated unfairly. Listen carefully, speak truthfully, and take a fair, practical step—at home, at work, or in your community.
- **Love mercy:** Choose one person to meet with patience or kindness, especially where you might usually criticize, keep score, or hold a grudge. Mercy doesn’t mean pretending harm is harmless; it means responding with compassion and wisdom.
- **Walk humbly with God:** Set aside a few quiet minutes each day to pray honestly and ask, “God, help me see what is good and do it today.” Be willing to receive correction and to ask forgiveness when needed.

The chapter contrasts elaborate offerings with the life God desires. The point isn’t to earn God’s favor through a perfect week, but to let gratitude for God’s faithfulness shape how you treat people. At the end of each day, you might ask: **Where did I practice justice? Where did I show mercy? Where do I need God’s help tomorrow?**

“The Word” is Jesus Christ—the Son of God. John doesn’t name him in verse 14, but the prologue identifies him through what it says about the Word: he was with God and was God, and all things were made through him (John 1:1–3). The Word is not merely a message from God; he is a divine person who reveals God.

The prologue builds toward the astonishing statement that “the Word became flesh, and lived among us” (John 1:14):

- The Word is present “in the beginning,” before creation (John 1:1–2).
- Everything was made through him, and in him are life and light (John 1:3–5).
- John the Baptist is sent to bear witness to the light, not to be the light himself (John 1:6–8).
- The true light enters the world, though many fail to recognize or receive him. Those who do receive him are given the right to become God’s children (John 1:9–13).

Verse 14 brings these themes together: the Creator and life-giving light comes close as a human being. “Lived among us” conveys God dwelling with his people; the glory, grace, and truth of God are encountered in the Son. In the wider biblical story, this is the fulfillment of the hope that God would dwell among his people—now not merely in a place, but personally in Jesus.

The main point is clear in the verse itself: the father sees his son “while he was still far off,” is “moved with compassion,” and runs to meet him. The son is returning ashamed and prepared to ask for a servant’s place, but the father acts before the son can make that offer. His embrace and kiss show welcome, not a cold hearing or a probation period.

That makes the running a vivid picture of the chapter’s larger theme: God’s joy in welcoming the lost who turn back. Jesus has just spoken of the shepherd and the woman searching for what was lost; now the father’s compassion brings that welcome close and personal. For anyone afraid to return to God, this scene offers hope: repentance matters, but the Father’s mercy is already reaching toward the repentant.

text:
John 1:5 says, “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness hasn’t overcome it.”

In the verses just before it, John describes the Word—who is God and through whom all things were made—as the source of life and “the light of men” (John 1:1–4). So the light in verse 5 points to God’s life and truth shining into a world marked by darkness: sin, suffering, and spiritual blindness.

The verse also carries a promise: darkness does not defeat the light. In the wider story of Scripture, God repeatedly brings light and life where there is darkness; John’s Gospel presents Jesus as that life-giving light. This doesn’t mean hardship disappears, but it means evil and despair do not have the final word.

When you face a dark or uncertain season, this verse invites you to hold on to the hope that God’s light continues to shine.

The text doesn’t tell us why Orpah chose differently. Naomi urged both women to return to their mothers’ homes and seek new lives, and Orpah eventually kissed Naomi and went back to her people and her god (Ruth 1:8–15). Ruth, by contrast, clung to Naomi and made a lasting commitment to her.

The passage does not explicitly call Orpah wrong or condemn her. Naomi’s words show compassion for both daughters-in-law, and Orpah’s farewell may have been a painful but understandable response to Naomi’s urging. Ruth’s choice is distinctive: she binds herself not only to Naomi but also to Naomi’s people and God. The story draws attention to Ruth’s extraordinary loyalty without requiring us to judge Orpah harshly.

No. Genesis 1:1 declares that God created the heavens and the earth, but this verse does not state when that happened or give the earth’s age.

Some Christians understand the creation account as describing six ordinary days and use genealogies elsewhere in Scripture to estimate a relatively recent creation. Other Christians understand the days or the passage’s structure differently, while affirming that God is Creator. The age of the earth is therefore an interpretation drawn from broader questions about Genesis and Scripture, not something Genesis 1:1 proves by itself.

At this verse, the central emphasis is that everything begins with God: the world is created, not self-existent or beyond his care.

## Exodus 3:1–14: The burning bush conversation

The scene begins in an ordinary task—Moses tending a flock—and becomes an encounter with the God who sees Israel’s suffering and commissions Moses to act. I’ll follow the verses in order, then look more closely at the Hebrew behind the divine name in verse 14.

### Verses 1–3: An unexpected sight

**Verse 1 — Moses at Horeb**  
Moses is shepherding the flock of his father-in-law, Jethro, in Midian. He leads it to “the back of the wilderness,” to Horeb, called “God’s mountain.” The setting is remote and quiet, far from Pharaoh’s court and Israel’s forced labor. Moses’ life has taken an unexpected turn: the man who once lived in Egypt is now a shepherd in Midian.

**Verse 2 — The bush that burns but is not consumed**  
Yahweh’s angel appears in a flame within a bush. The bush burns, yet it is not consumed. The text presents this as a “great sight,” but it does not explicitly explain the bush as a symbol. At minimum, it marks the encounter as extraordinary: Moses sees a fire that does not behave as fire normally does.

**Verse 3 — Moses turns aside to look**  
Moses decides to investigate why the bush is not burning up. His curiosity brings him near—but the encounter is not merely something he observes. God sees him approach and calls to him.

### Verses 4–6: God calls Moses and makes the ground holy

**Verse 4 — “Moses! Moses!”**  
God calls Moses by name, repeating it. Moses answers, “Here I am.” The call is personal, and the response is attentive: Moses makes himself available before he knows what God will ask.

**Verse 5 — “Don’t come close”**  
God tells Moses not to approach further and to remove his sandals, because the ground is holy. Holiness here is not something Moses creates; the place is holy because God is present. Removing his sandals is a bodily expression of reverence and awareness that he stands before the Holy One.

**Verse 6 — The God of the ancestors**  
God identifies himself as “the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” This connects the encounter to Israel’s earlier story. The God speaking from the bush is not a new deity but the God bound to the family and promise remembered through the patriarchs.

Moses hides his face because he is afraid to look at God. The scene holds reverence and relationship together: God calls Moses by name, yet Moses recognizes that he is in the presence of someone utterly holy.

### Verses 7–10: God sees, hears, knows—and sends

**Verse 7 — God knows their suffering**  
God says he has “surely seen” Israel’s affliction, heard their cry, and knows their sorrows. The wording is emphatic: Israel’s suffering is not hidden or forgotten. God names what is happening under the taskmasters and responds as one who is attentive to the people’s pain.

**Verse 8 — God will deliver and bring them to a good land**  
God says, “I have come down to deliver them” and to bring them into a “good and large land,” described as flowing with milk and honey. The movement is both away from oppression and toward a place of life and provision. The passage names peoples already living in that land; the promised destination is not empty, and the story will later have to confront the reality of entering it.

**Verse 9 — The cry has reached God**  
God repeats that Israel’s cry has come to him and that he has seen their oppression. The repetition underscores the basis for what follows: Moses’ mission begins because God has heard and seen the people’s plight.

**Verse 10 — Moses is sent to Pharaoh**  
God’s answer to Israel’s suffering includes sending Moses: “I will send you to Pharaoh.” God is the deliverer, but Moses is commissioned as the human agent who will confront Pharaoh and lead the people out. The mission is enormous, and Moses immediately recognizes the gap between the scale of the task and his own sense of himself.

### Verses 11–12: Moses’ question and God’s promise

**Verse 11 — “Who am I?”**  
Moses asks who he is to go to Pharaoh and bring Israel out of Egypt. It is a question about adequacy and authority. God does not answer by listing Moses’ abilities or assuring him that he is secretly powerful. Instead, God answers with a promise of presence.

**Verse 12 — “Certainly I will be with you”**  
God says, “Certainly I will be with you.” This is the central reassurance for Moses’ calling: the mission rests not on Moses’ self-confidence but on God’s presence.

The sign will be that, after bringing the people out, they will serve God on this mountain. It is a sign that will be fully recognized after the deliverance has happened. At this point Moses must trust God’s word before he can see its completion.

### Verses 13–14: Moses asks God’s name

**Verse 13 — “What should I tell them?”**  
Moses anticipates a question from the Israelites: if he says, “The God of your fathers has sent me,” they may ask, “What is his name?” In the ancient setting, a name could identify someone and tell people whom they were dealing with. Moses is asking how he should present God’s identity and authority to Israel.

**Verse 14 — “I AM WHO I AM”**  
God answers:

> “I AM WHO I AM,”

and tells Moses to say, “I AM has sent me to you.”

The Hebrew phrase is **אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה**, commonly transliterated **’ehyeh ’asher ’ehyeh**. **’Ehyeh** is a form of the Hebrew verb *hayah*, “to be” or “to become.” In this sentence it is often rendered “I am,” but its form can also be understood as “I will be.” The word translated **“who”** or **“that”** is *’asher*, so the phrase may be rendered in more than one way, including “I am who I am” or “I will be what I will be.” No single English rendering captures every nuance with certainty.

In context, the phrase is not an abstract definition detached from the story. Moses has asked how to speak of God to an oppressed people, and God has already promised him, “I will be with you” in verse 12. The wording in verse 14 echoes that promise: God’s identity is bound up with his faithful presence and action. He is not a powerless name Moses can wield; he is the living God who will be present with Moses and act to deliver Israel.

The next verse, **Exodus 3:15**, gives the name **Yahweh** and identifies the speaker as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The relationship between **’ehyeh** (“I am” or “I will be”) and **Yahweh** is widely recognized, though the precise derivation and full force of the divine name are not something to state with absolute certainty. The chapter itself places the two closely together: God’s self-declaration in verse 14 leads directly into the name Moses is to speak in verse 15.

## The movement of the passage

The conversation moves from **sight** to **calling**, from **calling** to **commission**, and from **Moses’ uncertainty** to God’s promise of presence:

- Moses sees the bush, and God calls him.
- God identifies himself as the God of the ancestors.
- God declares that he has seen, heard, and known Israel’s suffering.
- God commissions Moses to confront Pharaoh.
- Moses asks, “Who am I?”
- God answers, in effect, “I will be with you.”
- Moses asks for God’s name, and God reveals himself in a way that emphasizes his living, faithful presence.

The burning bush encounter therefore concerns more than Moses’ personal calling. It is God’s response to an enslaved people, and Moses is sent into that work with God’s presence as his assurance. For a reader today, the passage offers a grounded encouragement: Scripture does not say that suffering is unseen or that every calling feels easy. Here, God names Israel’s pain and sends Moses with the promise that he will be with him.

Romans 9:13 is a stark quotation, and Paul has just stressed that Jacob and Esau had done nothing good or bad when God’s purpose in election was announced (vv. 10–12). In context, he is explaining how God’s promise and calling—not ancestry or human achievement—shape the story of his people.

The words “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” come from the Old Testament book of Malachi (Malachi 1:2–3). There they speak about Israel and Edom, the peoples descended from Jacob and Esau, and God’s dealings with them across generations. So Paul uses the language of love and hate to make a forceful contrast about God’s choosing and covenant purposes; it should not be too quickly read as a claim that God feels personal malice toward a newborn.

Paul anticipates the troubling question this raises: “Is there unrighteousness with God?” His answer begins in the next verse: “May it never be!” (Romans 9:14). The passage does not invite us to conclude that God is cruel or that we can identify particular people as rejected from birth. It calls us to wrestle honestly with God’s sovereignty while trusting his character.

If this verse troubles you, that concern is understandable. Read it alongside the wider witness of Scripture to God’s justice and mercy, and remember that Paul’s grief for his fellow Israelites fills the chapter (Romans 9:1–3). The verse is part of a difficult argument, not a reason to despair about God’s heart toward you.

Peter has just confessed that Jesus is “the Christ, the Son of the living God” (v. 16), and Jesus says this was revealed by the Father (v. 17). So the “rock” may be understood as Peter, as Peter’s confession, or as Peter in his role as the first apostolic witness to that confession. The verse also makes clear that Christ is the one who builds the assembly.

Catholics read this passage, together with Matthew 16:19, as giving Peter a unique authority that continues through the popes. Many Protestant traditions affirm Peter’s important role but do not see this verse as establishing the papacy or its later claims. So Matthew 16:18 supports Peter’s special significance, but whether it proves that the Pope is right depends on broader questions about apostolic succession and church authority—not on this verse alone.

The central encouragement in the passage is that Jesus builds and sustains his people. The powers of death will not overcome his assembly.
